key_insight: LLM confidence reflects two competing biases: a choice-supportive bias that inflates confidence in initial answers, and a systematic overweighting of contradictory advice that causes departures from Bayesian-optimal updating.
problem_solved: Explains why large language models can display both overconfidence and underconfidence and why their confidence updates diverge from normative (Bayesian) reasoning.
method: Use an answer–advice paradigm: elicit an initial answer and confidence, present confirming or contradicting advice, then measure updated confidence.
Quantitatively compare LLM confidence updates to a Bayesian ideal observer to identify systematic deviations.
Analyze the pattern of deviations to dissociate a choice-supportive bias (boosting initial answers) from an overweighting of contradictory advice.
impact: Helps practitioners interpret and calibrate LLM confidence scores, and guides development of training, prompting, or post-hoc correction strategies to improve reliable human–AI decision-making.
visual_elements: Schematic showing competing biases: arrow from initial choice (choice-supportive) boosting confidence vs arrow from contradictory advice overweighting update
Line/bar chart comparing observed confidence updates to Bayesian-optimal updates for confirmatory and contradictory advice
Flow diagram of the experimental protocol (initial question → initial confidence → advice → updated confidence)
Icon set: calibration gauge, bias/brain symbol, and Bayesian scale to emphasize interpretation and corrective actions
paper_title: Competing Biases underlie Overconfidence and Underconfidence in LLMs
paper_authors: Dharshan Kumaran, Stephen M. Fleming, Larisa Markeeva, Joe Heyward, Andrea Banino
